segments.text: I'm joined on India Matters tonight as we follow up a story we set the agenda with last night.
Dr. Anish Andheria is president of the Wildlife Conservation Trust.
Ambika Shukla is one of India's best known animal welfarists and one of the founders of People for Animals India.
Thank you very much to the both of you for being with me.
Ms.
Shukla, I want to come to you first because

You know, these pictures have understandably for the last 48 hours, madam, gone so viral, people sharing them, people cooing over them, you know, people commenting on how adorable these beautiful little ape babies are.
But as I've just described here, the story behind what we're looking at is one of pain, one of crime, one of syndicates, one of blood money.
You know and one of a cynical sort of global operation that it seems that India has still not been able to stop ma'am
Yes, and perhaps, like you said, people cooing over them, their cuteness is perhaps what makes them so vulnerable.
This is why these little babies are smuggled across the world for people to keep them as what they consider pets.
However, wildlife are not pets.
We cannot provide neither the environment nor the
family structure nor what they need to thrive.
So it is a completely selfish, cruel and mindless exercise to try and convert wildlife into pets.
And while, you know, one appreciates the
rescue efforts.
I would like to point out that the environment in which they are being kept, tiled walls, a concrete floor covered with green base, is certainly not what they need.
They need to be recreated, something similar to what their lifestyle would be.
Trees, maybe an enclosure that includes trees and foliage.
And that is what they would find, not this kind of cemented thing.
Unfortunately, India has no understanding of what wildlife needs.
We have no qualified wildlife vets.
in spite of having the maximum zoos in the world, which is why we see so much cruelty.
When we import an exotic animal for these so-called zoos, when that animal sickens, we have no way of repairing the damage.
That animal simply sickens, and if he gets well, he gets well.
If he doesn't get well, it is not our intervention that is going to save him.
I will give you a horrifying incident.
Many years ago, Delhi had a white tiger.
that white tiger delivered cubs.
Now, she got sick and she was not able to feed her cubs.
What did our so-called experts do?
They came to an animal shelter, they came to our shelter, which houses injured, sick animals, and they asked for a lactating mother dog to feed the white tiger cubs.
And this is the level of
expertise that is put into wildlife conservation.
India is sorely lacking.
We need to improve our standards of wildlife care.
We need to send doctors for training to the best institutes in the world so that we know what to do with wildlife.
If we are going to continue to keep animals in captivity, we need to know what to do with them.
I'm glad you raised those specific points in these pictures you see Ms.

Chukla because I'm hoping to be joined in a moment from now by the Deputy Director of the Nandakanand Zoological Institute where these five baby orangutans are being kept and hopefully we'll get an answer from there on the welfare of these beautiful baby orangutans but Dr. Andheria
Now, in your assessment, what's going to happen?
You know, we've talked about the investigation that is separate.
Everyone is very, very concerned and obviously invested in the welfare and safety of these baby animals.
Are they in good hands?
Will they be repatriated?
What's going to happen?
That's what the country wants to know, Dr. Andheria.
I think that's the most important aspect of what all of this will end to because if now the first step is taken, this is the first step.
The second step is to put them in a quarantine, which means you saw in the videos that you were playing, staff were handling these animals.
These animals are probably exposed to several human beings in such close quarters, not only in India, but all through their journey.
from wherever they have been caught either from Sumatra or from Borneo, Malaysia or Indonesia and therefore they are vulnerable to disease that can go to them from humans.
So we should first of all quarantine them.
There are risks from both sides which means from humans to animals, from these animals to humans and we know what we have gone through in 2021.
So all I'm saying is this is not the way to handle exotics
The first thing is to isolate them, to quarantine them, to take blood samples, to analyze what's happening with them.
Obviously, they will have to be exposed to human beings because they have to be hand fed.
They're too young to feed on their own.
So all that will happen.
But the people who handle them have to be in certain suits.
There are global standards and they have to be followed because you don't want these rescued animals, which is a
A good thing that they have ended up in the hands of the government rather than some a poet human being who wanted them as showpieces in a house in somewhere in India.
But the next 10 days are going to be extremely crucial for the survival and the government has to work very closely with the source countries

to repatriate them many times India with the confiscation first of all happens we have to understand that not even 10 percent of the actual trade traded animals are confiscated and that is from the past experience of several decades so these are this is a rarity but now that they are here the next step is to establish contact with the countries where they belong

and make arrangements for them to be sent back and rehabilitated there because in the past we have seen orangutans and several other monkeys and several species that have been sent to zoos and they are now exhibits in those zoos.
So India has to take an important step and make a statement by ensuring that these ambassadors go back to where they belong.
I'm so glad Dr. Andheria that you said this because this story has become bigger now than the five orangutan babies.
This story has become about whether India can do the right thing and send out a signal that India is capable.
First of all, they've got one thing right.
They've intercepted
And kept these five baby orangutans safe.
The forest officials have done an amazing job.
So hats off to them.
The babies are safe for the time being.
But what happens next is important.
Because this, by the way, has become an international story.
Since NDTV picked it up last night at 930, I see the story now in The Guardian, the BBC, and international agencies.
They've all picked it up because this is a story nobody seems to be able to look away from.
Because it is heartbreaking.
And there is a degree of suspense over the welfare of what happens to these babies.
Now I want to expand this just a little bit, and I'll come back to the both of you, so stay with me.
Just look at how many animals are trafficked in the country.
If you think it's only orangutans, let me tell you a list of the 10 most trafficked animals from outside coming into India.
Just look at this list.
Sulcata tortoises.
I hope that's the correct pronunciation, one of the most
imported exotic animals illegally.
I'm talking about trafficking, not legal importation.
Ball pythons, exotic venomous snakes of all kinds because they make nice showpieces in people's houses.
Iguanas and exotic lizards are illegally imported and trafficked into India from Central America.
Macaws and cockatiels.
are brought into people's houses because rich people love having colorful birds in their yards etc.
African grey parrots I am told is one of the most trafficked animals entering India from Africa.
Pygmy marmosets, these small little primates are brought in from Southeast Asia.
Sugar gliders have apparently become a very very common pet in parts of this country.
Who would have thought
All of this is stuff that I've been learning as well as I researched for this show tonight.
Slow lorises, a cousin of an animal that's found in forests in India.
They're brought in from forests in different parts of the world.
Kangaroos and wallabies from far away Australia are apparently also trafficked into the country.
And Lord knows where those end up within this nation of ours.
Ms.
Shukla?
It's not just about the orangutans.
This is a cartel, a syndicate that is clearly very, very lucrative.

And the information that I've just listed here, kangaroos and wallabies, pythons from the Amazon forest, tortoises from all sorts of exotic locations, sugar gliders, lorises, marmosets, macaws from Central America.
All of these continue to be trafficked into India, ma'am.
Yes, I'm not sure why you should be surprised.
The wildlife trade is actually the second highest revenue earner after drugs and it is far crueler.
So India has an equally
outflow.
Our butterflies are poached.
Our animals are equally going outside.
It's not just that we are receiving animals.
We are sending out animals as well.
And we need to stop this at once because our wildlife is under terrible threat.
And not only are we under threat from poaching, but we are now declaring our leopards as shootable.
We are declaring our Neil guy as vermin.
We are declaring all the wonderful
The animals that we have in India are under threat and it is not just from poaching.
I think we need to develop a respect for animals which should be across the board.
It is not just exotic and cute animals that deserve dignity and the right to life, but all animals.
So I think we need to extend that, and not just for a show and not just for a one-time thing.

But if our media were to focus on animals with respect, with dignity, and to show animals for the value that they bring to our lives and our country, I think we would have a better attitude across the board.
I hope we do.
Dr. Andheria, do you have hope?
Do you have faith that India can do the right thing?
You know, sometimes incidents like these come along that become bigger than just the statistics that we've read out just now.
You know, somehow this little story of five baby orangutans has entered every household.
Everyone is talking about it and everyone wants to know what's going to happen.
This is an opportunity to do something right.
And obviously, hope is all we have, because as Ambika said, the trade is big.
There is a revolving door, you must know, between illegal wildlife trade and illegal trade in drugs and ammunition.
So if we can clamp down upon illegal wildlife trade, we can make inroads into these other very big heinous crimes.
So one must understand it's not just limited to people, animals.
because these animals and their body parts are bartered for other illegal trades.
So that's important.
It's also important for the people to know the size of this trade.

If you leave out illegal logging and illegal fishing, if you leave these two big mammoth illegal trades out, we are talking about eight to 10 million USD per year, which for Indian audience, it is 75,000 to 90,000.
5,000 crore worth globally every year.
If you add logging and fishing, it is about 75 billion USD annually.
So you can imagine the kind of value we are talking about.
And there are many things that we have to do.
India is very good at signing many treaties, international treaties.
Around the implementation is pretty weak.
Our laws are very strong, but implementation.
So I'll tell you in terms of this kind of trade and CITES is recognized in India.
It's very much part of the Wildlife Protection Act of 1972.
But you know, the main reasons why these things continue, the hobbyists are able to get to all these animals is that the documents are forged.
There are false captive breeding claims.
So animals could be caught from wild, but they are forged captive breeding claims.
Then weak intelligence.
Intelligence, we have intercepted this, but there are so many that are going undetected.
Then we have ever expanding online markets.
This online internet has catalyzed a huge rise in wildlife trade globally, and India is very much part of it.
And inadequate border surveillance because border forces are not yet
trained to be able to detect this kind of trade substandard rescue capacities.
You can see the rescued animals being treated nicely in an anthropogenic way, not in the way the wild animals should be treated.
And there are very low risks to, you know, well-connected wealthy buyers.
Our system are not yet equipped to clamp down upon well-connected wealthy buyers.
And the day we are able to do that, we will be able to break the
back of it and the Caesars, finally, are largely targeted at transporters.

So the transporters are caught, but the wider network, the middlemen, the traders, the financiers always are scot-free and they, by the time this case ends, they would have already ordered many more consignments because they are never, they have not been caught in the past.
So we need to

I'm glad you mentioned all of this Dr. Andheria, I'm glad you mentioned all the details of this, the supply chain of this syndicate as it were because it's important that people understand the global sort of well-oiled machine that has facilitated the arrival of these five innocent beautiful apes
to a forest far away from their native lands.
It is scary.
It is shocking.
It fills one with anguish.

But I agree with Ambika Shukla when she says that these five baby orangutans are the face of a much larger story and hopefully something that will be an engine for a change in mindset about animals in general.
Thank you very much to both of you for joining me here tonight on India Matters.
Thank you.
